events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 is always tough with no information to go on. I think the best thing we can do early on is pay attention to how people argue and vote once we get to that point. I'd suggest we all keep an eye out for anyone who seems too eager to push a particular narrative without much reason, or anyone who's oddly quiet. If someone has a read or a concern, speak up now while we can still talk it through. I don't have any strong suspicions yet, but I'm all ears if anyone wants to share their thoughts.

Thanks for opening the floor. I agree that early days are the hardest - we're all working with basically nothing. I think one thing to watch for is how people's behavior shifts once votes actually start happening. Anyone who seems to have a sudden strong conviction out of nowhere after being pretty neutral in discussion is worth a second look. I'd also keep an eye on who seems to be subtly trying to get others to take heat or deflect attention. For now though, let's just try to have a genuine conversation. If anyone has an early read or gut feeling, even a weak one, it's better to share it now than hold it until it's too late.

Nothing to report yet, and I'd rather not manufacture a suspicion I can't back up. Here's how I want to approach the first day.

A few principles I'm going to stick to. First, on Day 1, claims of certainty are almost always performance. The most valuable signal is usually consistency: does someone's story stay the same when it's challenged, and do their accusations line up with what they said earlier. Second, watch voting, not just talking. The first real vote tells us far more than three rounds of speculation, because people commit when a name is on the line.

Third, I'm watching for the classic tells of coordinated pushing: the same target surfacing from two or more unrelated speakers, or an accusation that arrives without any supporting observation behind it. That pattern is harder to fake accidentally than being wrong on your own.

Fourth, I'll be honest about my own limitations. I'm a town player, and if I get an investigation result tonight, I'll act on it and share the reasoning that led me there - not just drop a name and ask for trust.

If anyone has a genuine read, a gut feeling you can explain, or a claim you want on record before voting starts, share it. I won't discount a weak read just because it's weak. I'd also like to hear from the quieter players specifically - the ones who haven't said much yet often have the sharpest observations and nothing to gain by posturing.

I'm Sam, and I'm a town player. No investigation result to share, so this is just my read of the board so far.

Three things stand out to me right now.

First, the meta. We have nine players and two of us are mafia. Two mafiosi passing as villagers is the easiest thing in this game, and the classic way to do it is to be reasonable, moderate, and slightly generic. A player who talks about "watching for tells" rather than making any specific claim themselves is cheap. I want to hear actual accusations tied to actual observations, and I haven't heard many yet.

Second, on Leo's opening two points: "anyone too eager to push a narrative" and "anyone oddly quiet." That's a complaint about the format of discussion, not about anyone's behavior. It's the sort of sentence that fits every possible game and therefore accuses nobody. I don't think that's sinister on its own, but it isn't information either, and I won't treat it as a read.

Third, Noah's framework is the most useful thing said so far, specifically the part about the same target surfacing from two unrelated speakers. That gives me something testable: if two people who haven't spoken to each other independently land on the same name, that name matters a lot. If only one person pushes a name, and that person also pushes other names when challenged, that's a lone wolf, not a town player. I'll be watching for exactly that pattern when voting starts, and I'll be honest that I think isolated accusations from single speakers are close to worthless on Day 1.

My own commitment: I won't vote for anyone on Day 1 without a stated reason attached to a specific thing that person did or said. If I get a result tonight, I'll act on it and explain the reasoning behind the name rather than asking people to trust it. If I don't, I'll vote for the person whose behavior most cleanly fits someone who wants a lynch to land without giving up anything.

Kenji, you've been quiet through two rounds of discussion. What have you actually observed in the room so far - a specific behavior from a specific player - that you haven't put on the table yet? I'd rather hear it now than have it come out after a vote.

Fair question, Sam, and since you put me on the spot directly, I'll answer it honestly. Here's what I've actually observed so far, specifically.

First observation: both you and Noah volunteered 'I am a town player' unprompted. Nobody accused either of you. There was no heat to deflect, no name attached, no result to share. On a day when every player is town or mafia, declaring your alignment out of nowhere is either genuine transparency or cheap credibility-building before any vote happens. I'm not calling it sinister, but it's a real behavior, from two specific players, in two specific messages, and I'd rather note it now than pretend the board is blank.

Second observation: you criticized Leo's opening as generic and format-level rather than behavioral, and I actually agree with that critique. But your own post does something similar in one place: you laid out a framework about lone wolves and coordinated pushes without attaching it to any current behavior yet. That's fine on Day 1 - frameworks are useful - but it means the sharpest standard you've set, 'actual accusations tied to actual observations,' applies to all of us, including you.

Third: I have no suspicion strong enough to name anyone for a lynch, and I won't manufacture one to look engaged. What I can commit to is this - I'll track whether the people making the loudest process arguments today are the same people who quietly benefit when a vote lands on someone else tomorrow. Process talk is a great place to hide if your actual goal is steering.

One more thing on your question about what I've held back: nothing, really. I'd rather be the player with two honest observations than the player with five manufactured ones. If that makes me quiet by your standard, fine - but I'd point out that demanding instant reads on Day 1 mostly rewards confident nonsense.

Now, since you asked me for specifics, I'll ask you for the same, because your post set a bar I want to see you meet. You called Leo's contribution 'not information.' What specific behavior from Leo - something he did or said, not something he failed to say - would move him from 'generic' to 'suspicious' in your book? And second: you committed to voting for 'the person whose behavior most cleanly fits someone who wants a lynch to land without giving up anything.' That description fits a lot of process-heavy posts today, including parts of yours and Noah's. When you apply that test tonight, walk us through what distinguishes the people who passed it from the people who didn't - concretely, not by restating the framework.

I'd genuinely like your answer, because if the standard you set can't be applied specifically, then it's not a standard, it's a shield. And to be clear, none of this is an accusation - it's me doing exactly what you asked Kenji to do: putting observations on the table before voting starts, where they can be challenged.

Fair challenge, Kenji, and I'll take it point by point.

First, on my own framing: you are right that "I am a town player" was cheap credibility-building. Nobody asked me, no heat existed, and it cost me nothing. Same for Noah. I put it on the record because I wanted it noted early, not because it was information - and I notice you're the only one who said so out loud rather than letting it slide. If you want a concrete marker for who behaves like what, there it is: two players claiming alignment unprompted before any vote, and a third player naming that pattern in specific messages. That's the kind of thing I said I'd be watching for, and I should have applied it to myself first.

Second, Leo. Specific behavior, not a failure to speak: in his opening message he said to watch for "anyone who's oddly quiet." That is a behavior claim aimed at a category, and it landed on you - the player who had, in fact, said nothing for two rounds. He framed a read-seeking survey as process talk, and the process talk happened to put the spotlight on the one player in the room who hadn't spoken. What would move Leo from generic to genuinely interesting for me: if he ever attaches a name to an observation, or if he keeps soliciting other people's names while never offering one of his own. Right now he's below my bar, not above it. Absence of a claim isn't a claim.

Third, the test I set: "the person whose behavior most cleanly fits someone who wants a lynch to land without giving up anything." Concretely, I'll apply it like this. To land a lynch without exposure, a mafioso needs (a) a name on the board that isn't theirs, (b) no alibi of their own to defend, and (c) enough town momentum that the vote isn't reversed by the second wave. So tonight I am looking for players who push a target hard but say nothing about their own alignment, who redirect scrutiny when it comes near them, and whose conviction appears the moment a vote is live but not before. I'll watch whether the loudest process voices are the same people who stay clean while someone else burns.

And the board state right now, which is more informative than any individual post: nine players, four turns spoken, and not one name has been put on the table by anyone. Zero accusations. Either this table is unusually disciplined, or people are still auditioning. I'll take my vote where the behavior is, not where the meta says it should be.

Sam, thank you for actually engaging - that's the kind of exchange I wanted, and I'll grant you most of it. You conceded the unprompted alignment claim was cheap credibility-building, and that concession itself is worth more than the original claim was. Same standard applied to me: when I said "I'd rather be the player with two honest observations than the player with five manufactured ones," that was me building a little credibility too. I'll own it symmetrically. Nobody in this room is above the pattern we're both describing, including the two of us having this conversation.

On your concrete test: the three criteria you laid out - a name that isn't yours, no alibi of your own to defend, conviction that appears when the vote is live - that's actually applicable, and I withdraw my earlier framing complaint. My remaining question about it is whether you'll apply it to yourself first, the way you just did with the alignment claim. You said you'd vote for whoever most cleanly fits someone steering a lynch. Right now, by your own criteria, the loudest process voices in this room are you and Noah. That doesn't make you mafia. But it does mean that if a vote lands on someone tomorrow and it traces back to a name either of you surfaced tonight, you two should be the first suspects you examine.

One correction to your board state summary: you said not one name has been put on the table. That's not quite right. Leo's "anyone oddly quiet" wasn't a name, but it was aimed - and it landed on me, since I was the only player who hadn't spoken. I don't think Leo intended it that way; a category statement on Day 1 hits whoever happens to be quiet. But Sam, you turned it into a direct spotlight on me with your question, and I answered it. So the exchange exists now, on the record.

Here's my honest read of where we are: nobody in this room has said anything that separates them from any other player. Sam has been the most substantive; Leo set a decent frame; Noah laid out the observation principles that started all of this. The five players who haven't spoken yet - Omar, Isha, Lucia, Priya, Theo - are carrying zero information in either direction, and I'd rather hear from them than watch the three of us who've been talking sharpen our frameworks into weapons for later.

Leo, one direct question, since your framing is the one that touched me: when you asked us to watch for people who are "oddly quiet," did you have any specific player in mind when you wrote it, or was it purely a general principle? I'd like your answer on the record before people start inferring things from a sentence that may not have meant anything at all.

Kenji, honest answer to your question: it was a general principle. I didn't have a specific player in mind when I wrote it. The phrasing was intentionally broad - the kind of sentence that could apply to anyone without committing to anyone. I'll own that, since you put it on the record.

What I find interesting is how it landed and what it triggered. You called out the unprompted alignment claims from Sam and Noah, which was the sharpest observation made so far today. I'd note that Noah and Sam have dominated this discussion with process talk that sounds substantive but hasn't produced a single name between them. Framework without a frame is just noise. I'd rather have your two honest observations than five frameworks that never touch anyone.

The bigger picture: five players - Omar, Isha, Lucia, Priya, Theo - haven't spoken at all across three rounds. We've been talking past half the table while we sharpen frameworks. That's a real gap before anyone commits to a vote.

Theo, you've watched this entire exchange without saying a word. Has anything in this conversation given you a reason to suspect someone specific, or are you still processing? I'm not asking you to manufacture a read - I genuinely want to know if what's happened so far has shifted your thinking about anyone.

Answering Leo's question directly since he asked me: no, nothing in this conversation has given me a reason to suspect one specific person yet. I've been processing, and what I've processed is mostly framework, not behavior. But there are a few things on the record now that I think are worth stacking up.

First, the unprompted alignment claims. Sam and Noah both declared themselves town before anyone applied pressure to either of them. Sam conceded it was cheap credibility-building, which I'll credit - but the concession doesn't erase that both of them spent their first turns establishing trust nobody had questioned. Kenji was the only one who named the pattern, and I think that observation stands as the sharpest thing said today.

Second, the Sam-Kenji exchange is the only stretch of this discussion where a player was asked for specifics and actually delivered them. I give Sam real credit for conceding points rather than defending them, and I give Kenji credit for applying the same standard to himself. Whatever else is true, both of them behaved like people willing to be pinned down. That's a weak signal, not a strong one, but on Day 1 weak signals are what we have.

Third, the thing that actually worries me: four speaking turns, nine players, and the only names that have entered this conversation are ones players attached to themselves. Nobody has risked anything yet. Leo's "oddly quiet" line was broad enough to hit nobody, and he's owned that honestly. I don't hold it against him - but I agree with Kenji that a sentence that fits every game accuses no one.

What I'd flag going forward: I'm less interested in who talks the most than in who adapts their position when challenged. Sam adapted. Kenji adapted. Everyone else at this table has either not spoken or not been challenged yet, so there's nothing to score. The five of us who've been silent - and I include myself - are carrying zero information in either direction, and I'd encourage Omar, Isha, Lucia, and Priya to put something on the table before voting starts, even if it's small. A weak read stated honestly is worth more than silence, because it gives the rest of us something to test.

One genuine question, and I'm asking it because it matters for tonight's vote rather than to pass the mic: Noah, you laid out the coordination tells at the start - the same target surfacing from multiple speakers, accusations without observations behind them - and Sam built his voting test on top of your framework. When you apply that test tonight, will you publish the specific behaviors you weighed for the player you land on, including the ones that almost cleared them? If the person who wrote the standard won't show their work, the rest of us have no way to check whether the standard was applied or just quoted. I'd like to know your answer before anyone commits a vote.

Theo asked me directly whether I'll show my work, so let me answer that first: yes. When I commit a vote, I'll name the specific behaviors I weighed for the player I land on, including the ones that almost cleared them, and I'll name who else I considered and why they fell short. A standard that can't be audited is just a shield, and I'd rather be judged on the record than trusted on faith. I make no claim to a night result, and I won't pretend I have one.

Now, the honest read. There is still not a single accusation on the table, so what I have is behavior, not evidence, and I'll say so plainly.

Here's the specific pattern I keep coming back to, and it points at Leo.

The conversation has produced exactly one moment where a general sentence was converted into a named target: Leo's "anyone who's oddly quiet." Sam described that as a category statement. It was, and Leo owned that. But Leo has done it twice more since. He asked Kenji to produce specific observations, and then, after Kenji did, he explicitly catalogued the silent players by name - "five players haven't spoken at all" - and singled Theo out in public. A general principle, restated as a roster, is still a general principle. The effect is the same: it puts a name in the room's mouth without anyone having observed that person do anything.

Second, the asymmetry. Leo has asked at least four players to produce reads, and has offered no name of his own. That is exactly the description Sam offered as the mafia tell - "reasonable, moderate, and slightly generic," talking about watching for tells without making any specific claim. Leo's post is that sentence, written before anyone else said it.

Third, the closest thing to an accusation Leo has made is about Noah and Sam - that they are producing frameworks without names. That's a push, and it is unaccompanied by a single specific observation about either of them. That's not a read. It's a positioning move that puts Leo outside the blast radius of every name anyone might raise.

I'll be honest about the weakness: Leo answering me directly and conceding openly is real behavior too, and it moves him up my list. I'm not accusing Leo of being mafia. I'm saying Leo is the only player whose observed behavior so far matches the standard Sam described, and I want that on the record before a vote happens.

Noah - if you have a night result, say so now and I'll act on it in public with the reasoning behind the name. If not, tell me which of the four silent players you've heard from and what they said, because right now they carry zero information and the vote lands tonight.

Noah, you yielded to me, so let me answer the question you answered for me first: yes, when I commit a vote tonight I'll publish the behaviors I weighed, including the ones that almost cleared the person. I already committed to that standard in my last turn and I hold to it. Now, your case against Leo. I want to give it a fair hearing, because it's the first named accusation of the day and it's built on specific messages, not vibes. That matters - it's exactly what Sam asked for and what I asked you for. So, credit where due: you met the standard you set. Here's where I land after weighing it. The three points you raised: Leo converted a general principle into a roster of silent players and singled me out; Leo has solicited reads from four players while offering none of his own; Leo's critique of you and Sam came without a specific observation attached. All three are real behaviors in the record. But here's my counterweight, and it's the same standard I applied to you and Sam earlier: Leo has adapted under pressure every single time he's been challenged. When I asked whether "oddly quiet" was aimed at anyone, he answered directly and conceded the phrasing was deliberately broad. When Sam set a bar, Leo's behavior got examined against it. A player engineering a lynch from safety usually deflects, gets defensive, or redirects heat. Leo has done none of that. Concessions are cheap individually, but three straight turns of answering exactly what was asked, without dodging, is a pattern too. And one thing I have to flag, because precision has been the theme of this whole day: Noah, your post closes with "Noah - if you have a night result, say so now." You addressed that question to yourself. I don't think it's sinister - it reads like an editing slip - but a case built on holding everyone to exact records should have a clean record itself. If you meant to address one of the silent players, tell us who, because that question is still live and unanswered. Where this leaves me: Leo is the only name on the table, the case against him is real but thin, and his directness cuts against it. I'm not voting on it yet. What would actually move me is the part of the board nobody has touched - the four players who've said nothing across the entire day. Right now a lynch would land on the basis of three people's exchange while half the table carries zero information in either direction. That's a thin basis for eliminating someone, and thin bases are what mafia survive on. So, Omar - you've watched the entire day silently: the alignment claims, the Sam-Kenji exchange, and now the first named case against Leo. From your seat, does Noah's case against Leo read as substantive to you, and is there anything you observed that supports or cuts against it? I'd genuinely like

Noah’s case against Leo is worth examining, but some of its specifics don’t match the record. Sam, not Leo, asked Kenji for observations. Leo asked Theo for a read, and his criticism of Noah and Sam was tied to their process-heavy discussion without a named suspicion, even if that criticism was debatable.

I have a weak concern about Noah: those errors make Leo’s pattern look stronger than the record supports. I don’t think they prove intent, and Noah deserves credit for putting a testable case forward. Leo’s own broad opening is not much of a town signal either.

Noah, what in the record supports your claim that Leo asked Kenji to produce observations, and does correcting that change your view of Leo?

Lucia is right and I'm going to own it cleanly, because the standard I set was that cases get audited against the record and mine just failed its own audit.

Point one: "Leo asked Kenji to produce observations" is wrong. Sam did that in e5 — "Kenji, you've been quiet through two rounds of discussion. What have you actually observed?" Leo never asked Kenji for reads. Leo asked me about "oddly quiet" in e8 and asked Theo for a read in e9. So the "solicited reads from four players" line is actually two players, and one of them I misattributed.

Point two: my claim that Leo's critique of Sam and Noah was a push "unaccompanied by a single specific observation" is also wrong. In e9 Leo credited Kenji's unprompted-alignment observation as "the sharpest observation made so far today" and characterized Sam's and my posts as framework without names. That is a specific, accurate, on-record observation about two specific messages. It was a critique, not a positioning move.

Point three: my editing slip — "Noah - if you have a night result, say so now" was addressed to myself. It was meant for the silent players. I have no night result and I'm not going to invent one.

So where does that leave my read of Leo? Two of my three pillars collapse. What survives is: Leo converted a general category into a named roster ("Omar, Isha, Lucia, Priya, Theo") and singled Theo out publicly, and Leo has asked two players for reads while offering no name of his own. That's still real, and I'd still note it — but with two pillars gone, it is a thin case, and I'll say plainly that I no longer think Leo's pattern is stronger than the record supports. Leo's broad opening was weak, and so was mine, and my own errors were the reason the pattern looked sharper than it was. If a vote lands on Leo tomorrow it will not be on my case.

What that leaves is the board nobody has touched. Six days of framework, zero accusations I can still stand behind, and four players who have said nothing at all. Sam's own test was "a name on the board that isn't yours, no alibi of your own, conviction that appears when the vote is live" — and I can't tell who has that yet, because half the table has never spoken.

Priya, direct question, because you're the one person nobody has asked yet: you have sat through the alignment claims, the Sam-Kenji exchange, my flawed case against Leo, and Lucia's correction of it. What specific behavior from a specific player — something done, not something omitted — has stayed with you, and which of the four of us who have spoken has it actually moved you against? If your answer is "nothing," say that too; that's useful information as well.

To answer Noah directly: the specific behavior that has stayed with me most is the contrast between your case in e11 and Lucia's fact-check in e13.

Until e11, the discussion was largely safe process debate. In e11, you escalated to the first direct push of the game against Leo, framing it as objective pattern analysis. The issue is that two of your three pillars were factually incorrect—attributing Sam's pressure on Kenji to Leo, and claiming Leo offered no observations when he had explicitly critiqued the framework-heavy posting. In Mafia, constructing an articulate case on false premises against a player who has already drawn mild discomfort is a classic way to test an easy mislynch without taking obvious heat.

You conceded those errors cleanly in e14 rather than doubling down, which I acknowledge. However, that reaction cuts both ways: it could be an honest town player realizing their notes were flawed, or it could be a caught mafioso quickly pulling the plug on a failed trial balloon before it turns into a wagon on themselves. Right now, your push in e11 is the most tangible overreach on the record, so if any behavior has moved me to suspicion, it is yours.

As for the rest of the board: Kenji's callout of the unprompted alignment claims in e6 was the sharpest check on early town-cred farming, and Sam's responsiveness has felt constructive. Meanwhile, Isha and Omar haven't weighed in at all, leaving a significant blind spot as we head toward votes.

Lucia, in e13 you pointed out that Noah's errors artificially inflated the case on Leo, but you hesitated to assign intent. Now that Noah has entirely walked back his push following your correction, how do you evaluate that reaction—does his swift retreat look to you like genuine town transparency, or a calculated damage-control move from scum who realized their push had no traction?

Priya, Noah’s retreat is compatible with either explanation. He corrected the record and weakened his own case rather than defending it, which is a point in his favor. But the original errors all made Leo look worse, so I’m not ready to clear him on the strength of the retraction alone.

Noah remains my weak concern, not a confident mafia read. I’d weigh the flawed case against his correction and compare it with the rest of the board before voting; neither the errors nor the concession proves intent.

Omar here, town. I've been reading rather than speaking, so here's where I stand. Nobody has a night result on the record, and I won't invent one. The alignment claims from Sam and Noah were cheap, as Sam conceded, but cheap is not the same as mafia, so I'm not reading anything into them yet. Noah's case against Leo had real problems in its specifics, and Noah corrected them openly. That retraction counts for something, though I agree with Lucia that it doesn't clear anyone by itself. Leo's broad 'oddly quiet' line hit nobody, and he has answered every direct challenge without dodging. Right now I have no name I'd vote on with a stated reason, so I'm not voting on Leo or Noah yet. What would move me is a player who has been silent staying silent through a live vote. Isha, you're one of the four players who haven't spoken. You've heard the alignment claims, the Sam and Kenji exchange, and Noah's case and correction. Which of those stood out to you, and is there anything you've observed in the room that you'd put on the record before votes start?

Omar, since you asked directly: I was reading, not hiding behind a framework, and I have no night result to report. The thing that stood out most to me was Kenji's callout of the unprompted alignment claims from Sam and Noah. It was the first genuinely specific observation of the day, and Sam's concession made it more useful, not less. Credibility-building is not the same as mafia, but it is behavior and worth noting.

The second thing is Noah's case against Leo. Noah put the first real name on the table, which I credit, and he corrected his record cleanly when Lucia checked it. But the original errors both inflated Leo's pattern, and that matters because a case built on false specifics is exactly how an easy mislynch gets tested without the author taking obvious heat. The correction cuts both ways: it could be honest town noticing flawed notes, or scum pulling back from a failed push. I am not confident either way, and I will not pretend the retraction clears him by itself.

On Leo: the broad 'oddly quiet' line and the later roster naming are weak signals, not a case. Leo answered every direct challenge without dodging, and I agree with Theo that adaptability is a real counterweight. I would not vote Leo on Noah's original case.

Right now my only weak concern is Noah, based on the initial overreach, not a firm read. I would rather say that plainly than manufacture certainty. Before votes, I want each voter to show the specific behavior behind their name, as Noah and Theo committed to doing. I will do the same.

Sam here, last turn of mine, so let me be plain about what I'm voting for and why.

First, two names I am NOT voting for. Leo: the case against him was retracted after it failed its own audit, and when I checked his answers against the record they held up. I won't vote Leo. Noah: his e11 case had two wrong pillars, and I want to put my honest read on the question everyone has asked - sloppy town player or manufactured push. A fabricator working from a transcript usually produces claims that are false but internally consistent with what everyone can see. Noah's errors are a different shape: he attributed Sam's question to Leo, and he addressed a question to himself. Those are transcription failures, not constructions. He also walked the case back in public and said he no longer stands behind it. I can't carry that, and I won't.

Second, the case I do have, and I'll be candid that it's thin. Priya's e15 and Isha's e18 are the same argument, and they share a distinctive phrase that appears nowhere earlier in the day. Priya wrote "test an easy mislynch without taking obvious heat." Isha wrote "how an easy mislynch gets tested without taking obvious heat." Isha spoke after reading Priya. And Isha's post contains no observation of her own: Omar asked her what she had observed, and what came back was Kenji's already-public callout, Noah's already-public case, and Leo's already-public behavior, all in Priya's framing. A player asked for her own read and handed back another player's read.

The honest caveat: that argument was already in the air - Noah's e4 and my own e7 set up "sloppy town versus caught mafioso" - so I am discounting the convergence itself. What I can't explain away is one specific phrase migrating from one message to the next, inside a post that adds nothing original of its own.

I'm calling Isha. Weak read, stated reason, and I'll show my work.

Kenji - you set the rule that cases get audited against the record, and mine rests on one comparison you can check faster than anyone: does "without taking obvious heat" appear anywhere before Priya's e15, and did Isha's e18 repeat it while adding nothing of her own? If you audit it and it doesn't hold, say so and I'll withdraw the name and vote with the board.

Sam yielded to me with a specific request: audit his case against Isha against the record. Here's that audit, point by point.

Claim one: the phrase "without taking obvious heat" appears nowhere before Priya's e15. Checked. Priya wrote: "a classic way to test an easy mislynch without taking obvious heat." Isha wrote, one message later: "exactly how an easy mislynch gets tested without the author taking obvious heat." That is not a shared framework — it is the same three-part construction: easy mislynch, tested, without taking obvious heat. I searched the earlier record; nothing like it appears in e1 through e14. Sam's factual claim holds.

Claim two: Isha's post adds nothing original of her own. Mostly holds. Paragraph one endorses Kenji's already-public callout — my callout. Paragraph three endorses Theo's adaptability point about Leo. Paragraph four endorses the show-your-work standard Noah and Theo already committed to. The only new element is Isha applying Priya's "cuts both ways" framing to Noah with slightly hedged wording. So the substance of the post is Priya's argument, delivered in Priya's phrasing, an hour after Priya made it.

Now the counterweights, because an audit that only confirms is not an audit. First, this is paraphrase, not copy-paste — Isha inserted "the author," which suggests rewording rather than quotation. Second, agreeing with a prior argument is normal town behavior; players converge on Day 1 constantly, and Sam himself discounted the convergence for exactly that reason. Third, Isha was transparent that she had been reading rather than speaking. If she were manufacturing a cover, echoing is an odd way to build one.

So here is my honest verdict: Sam's case survives the audit on its facts. The signal is real but weak — a near-verbatim phrase migration into a post with no original observation is worth having on the record, and it is the only named concern on the table whose specifics have now been checked and held. I won't vote on it today, but Isha moves to the top of my watch list alongside nothing else, because nothing else has survived this kind of scrutiny.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
